episodes.title: Why Humans Can't Keep Up With AI-Written Code - Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
episodes.description:
Agents have made code cheap: one study saw lines of code up 2,450% but releases up only 30%. Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat draws on the factory revolution that Toyota and Lexus started to explain how to build agentic software factories you can trust. He breaks down five hard problems: human review that doesn't scale (people agree with AI that's wrong 4 out of 5 times), agents struggling with large codebases, errors compounding over long tasks, unreliable LLM judges, and near-zero time to exploit. Then he lays out Sonar's code confidence formula: intent, guide rails, verification and evidence.

episodes.title: How Revolut Cut AI Coding Costs 90% With Self-Hosted Open Models - David Abitbol, Revolut
episodes.description:
David Abitbol, who leads AI operations at Revolut, shares data from 2,000 engineers on what AI tools did to coding time and lead time, and why self-hosting open-source GLM models made the biggest difference: about 60-70% faster delivery at roughly a tenth of what they were paying frontier labs. He covers the GPUs needed, the latency targets that keep engineers happy, the tuning that made the same hardware 88% faster, and how an EU-regulated bank keeps it compliant.

episodes.title: We Trust AI Agents That Break Every Day - Shy Ruparel, Temporal
episodes.description:
Temporal's State of Development survey found that 80.8% of engineers use agents daily, but only 49.1% run them in production. Developer advocate Shy Ruparel walks through the four gaps behind that number (usage vs. production, trust vs. reality, prototype vs. enterprise, seeing vs. recovering), then demos a $2,500 payout workflow with a local model that survives having its workers killed mid-flight, without losing state, repeating tool calls or re-spending tokens.

episodes.title: Why a One-Line Change Can Break Your Whole Stack - Cole Gannaway, Qodo
episodes.description:
Code generation is moving faster than ever, and the bottleneck has moved to review. Cole Gannaway, a solutions engineer at Qodo, shows how a one-line data model change that passes every test can quietly break web, mobile, CLI and MCP clients, and how a software graph of your repos reveals that blast radius. He covers turning tribal knowledge and PR comments into custom rules, bringing review context in before code is written, why the agent that wrote the code shouldn't grade it, and checking PRs against the original ticket.

episodes.title: How Anthropic Merges 30,000 Code Changes a Day - Manish Kapur, Sonar & Addy Osmani, Anthropic
episodes.description:
Coding agents are opening PRs faster than anyone can review them. Manish Kapur (Sonar) and Addy Osmani (Anthropic) discuss "light" vs. "dark" software factories, how Anthropic scaled from about 2,500 to 30,000 merged changes a day with Claude doing first-pass review backed by real verification evidence, new data from Sonar's State of Code survey, and why every loop in the factory needs independent, multi-layered verification. They close with a lightning round on labeling agent-written PRs and when it's safe to merge.

episodes.title: AI That Hunts Logic Bugs Before Attackers Do - Taylor Luttrell-Williams, Sonar
episodes.description:
Pattern-based SAST catches bad code, but not valid code with flawed intent: broken access control, business logic gaps and authentication holes. Taylor Luttrell-Williams of Sonar introduces the SonarQube Hunter Agent, which maps a repo, runs three specialist agents and adversarially validates every finding, and announces Sonar joining the OpenAI Daybreak cyber partner program. The live demo turns up 46 issues in a Python app, including a user who can make themselves admin and an MFA bypass.

episodes.title: Stop Guessing Your vLLM Config: Benchmarking LLMs on Runpod - Chris Vela, Runpod
episodes.description:
Most teams spin up a new open model with the default vLLM recipe and hope for the best. Runpod forward-deployed engineer Chris Vela shows how to choose configs from data instead, starting with the use case and concurrency, and demos BenchPod, a benchmarking dashboard built on vLLM that tests configs live without restarts. He runs Kimi K3 on a B300, shows how tuning max batch tokens cuts inter-token latency, and asks whether you need a frontier model at all.

episodes.title: Who Is Making This Request? Agent Auth 101 - Kamil Potrec, Keycard
episodes.description:
When an agent sends an invoice using your token, who actually made the request? Kamil Potrec of Keycard breaks down how agents get credentials today (personal tokens, static keys, over-privileged service accounts) and what proper agent auth requires: per-agent identity, delegation, short-lived scoped credentials, federation with legacy systems, policy and audit. He compares SDKs and gateways for keeping credentials out of an agent's reach, including the gateway tradeoffs.

episodes.title: Exploits Now Beat Patches: Open Source Security in the AI Era - Patrick Smyth, Chainguard
episodes.description:
Frontier AI has made every attacker a level more dangerous, and on average, exploits now land before the patch. Patrick Smyth of Chainguard covers this year's AI-assisted attacks and supply chain malware waves, why 30-day remediation windows no longer hold up, the four attack surfaces to cover (malware, known CVEs, zero days and "side doors" like CI/CD, developer laptops and agent skills), and what to do now: cooldown periods, faster CVE fixes, and signing everything with SLSA and Sigstore.

episodes.title: We Kept Rebuilding Our AI Agent. Here's What Survived - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
episodes.description:
Arize's in-product agent Alex went from a 2023 prototype that was "50% hallucination" to a single agent with planning, memory and on-demand skills, all built with custom harness code instead of a framework. AI PM Fuad Ali covers each decision: moving the plan into the harness, making "finish" an explicit gate, treating large tool results like files, why one 8,000-character memory file per user beat vector stores and knowledge graphs, merging 10 specialists into one agent, and using production sessions as tests.
